date.label: Undated Deuteronomic discourse and legislation
date.note: Biblical narrative chronology is not independently established as an absolute BCE date.

claims.claim: Moses spoke to all Israel on this side Jordan, in the land of Moab, in the fortieth year, in the eleventh month, on the first day of the month, after Sihon and Og were slain (Deut 1:1–5).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 1:1–5, read in full (BibleGateway KJV; Preview API raw data, 0 diffs vs BibleHub ch. 1).

claims.claim: “There are eleven days' journey from Horeb by the way of mount Seir unto Kadeshbarnea” (Deut 1:2).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 1:2, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: Moses appointed wise, understanding, known men as captains over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens, and charged the judges to judge righteously, “for the judgment is God's” (Deut 1:9–18).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 1:9–18, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) — for the quoted wording (“for the judgment is God's”); JFB on Deut 1:9–18 (Jethro reference).

claims.claim: Israel went from Horeb through “all that great and terrible wilderness” and came to Kadesh-barnea (Deut 1:19).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 1:19, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) — for the quoted wording (“all that great and terrible wilderness”); JFB on Deut 1:19–21 (wilderness of Paran; El Tih).

claims.claim: Twelve men, one of a tribe, were sent as spies; they went to the valley of Eshcol, brought fruit, and reported “a good land” (Deut 1:22–25).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 1:22–25, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The people would not go up but rebelled, murmured in their tents, and feared a people “greater and taller than we,” cities “great and walled up to heaven,” and “the sons of the Anakims” (Deut 1:26–28).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 1:26–28, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) — for the quoted wording (“greater and taller than we”; “great and walled up to heaven”; “the sons of the Anakims”); JFB on Deut 1:28 (Anakim; Heb 3:19).

claims.claim: The LORD swore that none of that evil generation would see the good land, save Caleb son of Jephunneh; Joshua would enter it; and the little ones would go in and possess it (Deut 1:34–39).
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 1:34–36, 1:39.

claims.claim: The people went up presumptuously after repenting, were chased by the Amorites “as bees do” and destroyed in Seir unto Hormah, and wept before the LORD, who would not hearken (Deut 1:41–45).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 1:41–45, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) — for the quoted wording (“as bees do”); JFB on Deut 1:40–45.

claims.claim: “So ye abode in Kadesh many days, according unto the days that ye abode there” (Deut 1:46).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 1:46, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) — the claim statement is a verbatim quotation; JFB on Deut 1:46.

claims.claim: Israel compassed Mount Seir many days, then was commanded northward, to pass through Esau's coast buying meat and water for money and not meddling with Edom, “these forty years… thou hast lacked nothing” (Deut 2:1–8).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 2:1–8, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) — for the quoted wording (“thou hast lacked nothing”); JFB on Deut 2:1, 2:5–7.

claims.claim: Moab was not to be distressed, for Ar was given to the children of Lot; the Emim dwelt there before, “a people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims,” and the Horim in Seir before Esau succeeded them (Deut 2:9–12).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 2:9–12, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) — for the quoted wording (“a people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims”); JFB on Deut 2:8–12.

claims.claim: “The space in which we came from Kadeshbarnea, until we were come over the brook Zered, was thirty and eight years; until all the generation of the men of war were wasted out” (Deut 2:14).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 2:13–16, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) — the claim statement is a verbatim quotation (Deut 2:14); JFB on Deut 2:13, 2:16.

claims.claim: Ammon was not to be distressed, for its land was given to the children of Lot; it was accounted a land of giants (Zamzummim), and the Avims in Hazerim were destroyed by the Caphtorims from Caphtor (Deut 2:19–23).
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 2:19–23.

claims.claim: Moses sent messengers from Kedemoth to Sihon with words of peace; Sihon refused, his spirit hardened; Israel smote him, his sons and all his people at Jahaz and took all his cities (Deut 2:24–33).
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 2:24–36.

claims.claim: From Aroer by the Arnon even unto Gilead no city was too strong for Israel; only Ammon, the Jabbok and the mountain cities were untouched (Deut 2:36–37).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 2:36–37, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: Og king of Bashan came out at Edrei; Israel took all his cities, “threescore cities, all the region of Argob,” fenced with high walls, gates and bars, and utterly destroyed them (Deut 3:1–7).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 3:1–7, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) — for the quoted wording (“threescore cities, all the region of Argob”); JFB on Deut 3:1–20.

claims.claim: Israel took the land of the two Amorite kings from the Arnon unto Mount Hermon, “which Hermon the Sidonians call Sirion; and the Amorites call it Shenir” (Deut 3:8–10).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 3:8–10, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) — for the quoted wording (“which Hermon the Sidonians call Sirion; and the Amorites call it Shenir”); JFB on Deut 3:9 (Jebel esh-Sheikh).

claims.claim: “Only Og king of Bashan remained of the remnant of giants; behold, his bedstead was a bedstead of iron… in Rabbath of the children of Ammon; nine cubits was the length thereof, and four cubits the breadth of it” (Deut 3:11).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 3:11, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) — the claim statement is a verbatim quotation; JFB on Deut 3:11.

claims.claim: The land from Aroer and half Mount Gilead was given to Reuben and Gad, the rest of Gilead and all Bashan to half-Manasseh; Jair took Argob (Bashan-havoth-jair) and Machir received Gilead (Deut 3:12–17).
The eastern tribes were to pass over armed before their brethren until the LORD gave them rest, their wives, little ones and cattle remaining in their cities (Deut 3:18–20).
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 3:1–20.

claims.claim: Moses charged Joshua from what his eyes had seen of the two kings, prayed to cross over and see the good land, was refused (“Let it suffice thee”), and was sent to the top of Pisgah to see it with his eyes (Deut 3:21–28).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 3:21–28, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) — for the Joshua charge (vv. 21–22) and the Pisgah view (vv. 27–28), which JFB does not cover (no Deut 3:21–29 entry in the restructured JFB data), and for the quoted wording (“Let it suffice thee”, v. 26); JFB on Deut 3:25–26 (the refused prayer).

claims.claim: “So we abode in the valley over against Bethpeor” (Deut 3:29).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 3:29, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The eleven days of Deut 1:2 are set against the forty years to show the delay was judgment for apostasy and rebellion, not the length of the way.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 1:2 (read in full): the days “were not necessarily successive days” (Robinson); “this mention of the time was made to show that the great number of years spent in travelling… was not owing to the length of the way, but to… banishment for their apostasy and frequent rebellions.” A commentary reading of the text's framing, not a measured itinerary.

claims.claim: The text's internal chronology is coherent: 38 years from Kadesh to the Zered (2:14) within the fortieth year of the speech (1:3), the difference being the time from the exodus to Kadesh.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 1:3; 2:14, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). Established as a textual fact; the absolute date is a separate claim (025).

claims.claim: The absolute date of the speeches is disputed: the traditional Mosaic dating is c. 1406 BCE (Matthew Henry's titles give 1451 BC), while most modern scholars date Deuteronomy's composition to the 7th–5th centuries BCE.
claims.evidence: Traditional side: Matthew Henry titles “(1451 BC)” (read in part); GotQuestions “When was Deuteronomy written?” (read in full — Moses wrote it “at the end of the 40-year period, around 1400 BC”; Deuteronomy identifies Moses as its author five times) and “Summary of the Book of Deuteronomy” (read in full — “The year was 1406 B.C.”). Modern side: Wikipedia “Book of Deuteronomy” (read in full — “most modern scholars date Deuteronomy to the 7th–5th centuries BCE”; “Virtually all modern secular scholars, and most Christian and Jewish scholars, reject the Mosaic authorship of the Book of Deuteronomy and date the book much later, between the 7th and 5th centuries BCE”; de Wette 1805; 7th-century Jerusalem composition under Hezekiah/Josiah; Weinfeld on the Esarhaddon-treaty affinities and the Josianic reform). No modern critical commentary (Weinfeld, Levinson, Tigay, Lundbom) was read directly in this session — the modern side rests on the Wikipedia overview (a tertiary summary citing Stackert, Weinfeld, Rofé, Tigay) and is disclosed as such; Bradshaw and Wikipedia “Composition of the Torah” remain search excerpts only and are no longer relied on for this claim.

claims.claim: Deuteronomy presents itself as Moses' farewell discourses, framed by third-person narration, with later editorial notices; no verse-by-verse date can be inferred for Deut 1–3 without arguments.
claims.evidence: Bible Odyssey, “Deuteronomy” dictionary entry (read in full) — “a series of three discourses by Moses (Deut 1:6–4:40; Deut 5–28; Deut 29–30); with a concluding addendum (Deut 31–34)”; corroborated by Wikipedia “Book of Deuteronomy” (read in full — three speeches 1:1–4:43, 4:44–29:1, 29:2–30:20 + epilogue 31:1–34:12). Scholarly Disagreement Register #6. The “no verse-by-verse date” rule is the register's, applied here.

claims.claim: Retrospective notices in Deut 1–3 (“unto this day,” 3:14; “as Israel did unto the land of his possession,” 2:12) indicate a narrator looking back after settlement — a later editorial hand within the speech.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 2:12, 2:22; 3:14, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) — for the quoted wording (“unto this day”; “as Israel did unto the land of his possession”); JFB on Deut 3:14 (read in full): “This remark must evidently have been introduced by Ezra, or some of the pious men who arranged and collected the books of Moses.” A commentary judgment; the hand is not dated by this dossier.

claims.claim: Deut 1:37 attributes Moses' exclusion to the people's sake (“the LORD was angry with me for your sakes”), while Num 20:12 attributes it to Meribah; the two accounts stand in tension.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 1:37, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) — for the quoted wording (“the LORD was angry with me for your sakes”); Num 20:12 cited from the parallel account, conn-deu-01-005; JFB on Deut 1:37 (read in full): the verse “must be considered therefore as a parenthesis” referring to the later event at the waters of strife (Ps 106:32–33). JFB's resolution is recorded as a commentary reading, not adopted as settled.

claims.claim: Kadesh-barnea is Tell el-Qudeirat: the leading candidate, accepted by most scholars, on the strength of the spring, the route position and the Iron Age remains.
claims.evidence: BAR, “Tell el-Qudeirat (Kadesh Barnea)” site page, read in full: proposed by Lawrence and Woolley 1914; “the identification is accepted today by most scholars, because of the spring, its location on major routes and the Iron Age remains”; Ein Qadis proposed as an alternative. No inscription names Kadesh at the site.

claims.claim: The excavated remains at Tell el-Qudeirat are Iron Age fortresses (10th–6th centuries BCE); no Late Bronze Age remains have been found there, and no excavated layer is tied to the narrated wilderness encampment.
claims.evidence: BAR site page, read in full: Cohen's three fortresses (elliptical 10th c.; two rectangular 8th c.–586 BCE); Ussishkin's single-fortress reading; Finkelstein's 10th–8th-c. settlement + mid-8th to late-7th-c. fortress; “The absence of Late Bronze Age remains at the site raises questions about the historical background of the wilderness traditions.” The negative fact is established; its implication for the narrative is Debated (see dossier §8.2).

claims.claim: Heshbon is Tell Hesban: the traditional identification, supported by the survival of the name at the ruin, Eusebius' distance (20 Roman miles from the Jordan), and the site's position on the plateau between Arnon and Jabbok.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining Library, “Heshbon”, read in full: “Its name survives at the ruin of Hesban… where excavations have revealed a long history”; Eusebius placed Esbus 20 Roman miles from the Jordan, “which agrees well with the location of the modern ruin.” The identification of the later (Roman/Byzantine Esbus) town is the secure part; see 032 for Sihon's city.

claims.claim: Sihon's Bronze Age Heshbon has not been found at Tell Hesban: no clear Late Bronze Age city was found, the earliest Iron Age settlement was modest, and the question remains open (Tell Jalul proposed as an alternative).
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining Library, “Heshbon”, read in full: “No clear remains of a Late Bronze Age city… were found at Tell Hesban, and the earliest Iron Age settlement appears to have been modest”; “The question remains open, and the archaeology alone cannot settle it.”

claims.claim: No extrabiblical inscription naming Sihon, king of Heshbon, was located in this research.
claims.evidence: Searches for Sihon/Heshbon epigraphy in this session returned no inscription; the claim is the absence of located evidence, not proof of non-existence. A specialist epigraphic check could revise it.

claims.claim: Ashtaroth is Tell Ashtara and Edrei is modern Der'a (Daraa) in southern Syria: the usual identifications.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining Library, “Og” (read in full): “Ashtaroth is usually located at Tell Ashtara and Edrei at modern Daraa, both in southern Syria.” The Thutmose III / Amarna attestation clause formerly in this claim was removed: the “Og” article does not state it, and the BiblicalTraining “Ashtaroth” article (read in full this session; not in §12 or the registry) states Thutmose III's “Ashtartu” and the Amarna letters generally but does NOT name EA 197 specifically. The Thutmose/EA 197 detail still needs a direct read of the lists or the letter before it is restored. Capped at Probable.

claims.claim: A Ugaritic text describes a divine figure dwelling in Ashtaroth and ruling in Edrei — the same pair of cities linked with Og in Deut 3 — converging with Deut 3:11's “remnant of giants”; scholars debate what the parallel means.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining Library, “Og” (read in full): “One Ugaritic text describes a divine figure as dwelling in Ashtaroth and ruling in Edrei, the same pair of cities linked with Og. Scholars debate what this parallel means.” The specific “ʿg mlk ʾdry” reading was NOT verified: the text is reported (search excerpt only, BibleHub evidence page) as KTU 1.108:26-28, and a search of the Wikipedia “Og” article found mainstream translations (Wyatt; del Olmo Lete) reading Rapiu (rpʾu), patron of the rpʾum/Rephaim, enthroned in Ashtaroth and ruling in Edrei — no “Og” personal name in the tablet as translated. The ʿg reading remains a reported reading for a Ugaritic specialist. Neither KTU 1.108 nor any scholarly edition was read directly; not presented as proof of Og's historicity.

claims.claim: The Transjordanian regional geography of Deut 1–3 — the Arabah, Mount Seir, the Zered, the Arnon, the Jabbok, Gilead, Bashan/Argob, Hermon, the Salt Sea and Chinnereth — is identifiable as the text describes it.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 1:2, 1:6, 2:1, 2:13, 2:24–36, 3:1, 3:9, 3:12–13 (read in full); BAR Tell el-Qudeirat page (read in full); BiblicalTraining “Heshbon” (read in full). Exception: Jabbok = Wadi Zarqa was not verified by a directly-read source in this session (shared record §7).

claims.claim: The route of the 38-year wandering between Kadesh and the Zered cannot be reconstructed from Deut 1–3.
claims.evidence: Deut 2:1 gives no itinerary; JFB on Deut 2:1 reconstructs a route south through the Arabah to the Gulf of Aqaba and back north along the hadji route — a reading, not an established fact; the Num 33 station list was not mapped to Deut 2 in this dossier.

claims.claim: The text presents the Emim, Zamzummim and Rephaim as earlier giant peoples displaced before Moab, Ammon, Edom and Israel (Deut 2:10–11, 20–21; 3:11, 13).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 2:10–11, 20–21; 3:11, 13, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). Established as a textual presentation; the Ugaritic rpum connection is Debated (see clm-deu-01-035).

claims.claim: The herem language of the Sihon and Og episodes states total destruction: “utterly destroyed the men, and the women, and the little ones, of every city, we left none to remain” (Deut 2:34; cf. 3:6).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 2:34; 3:6, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). Established as text; rhetoric, historicity and ethics are separate analyses (Phase 2 Correction Record; dossier §8.3).

claims.claim: The destructions of Sihon's and Og's cities have no independent archaeological or epigraphic confirmation located in this research.
claims.evidence: No inscription, destruction layer or battlefield evidence tied to Jahaz or Edrei was located in the sources read for this dossier (BAR, BiblicalTraining, JFB, Matthew Henry). The absence is recorded, not filled.

claims.claim: Og's bedstead is stated as nine cubits long and four broad, of iron, in Rabbath of the Ammonites; whether it was a bed, an oversized display bed, or a coffin is not settled.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 3:11 (read in full): the dimensions and the Rabbath location are stated in the text; the 11–12 ft estimate, the Alexander parallel, the Rabbath problem, and the “coffin” reading (Dathe, Roos) are all recorded as unresolved options.

connections.note: The appointment of judges; Jethro's advice is the occasion in Exodus, Moses' burden the emphasis here (JFB on Deut 1:9–18).
The spies sent to Eshcol; the good report. Initiative differs (people propose here, the LORD commands in Num 13:1–2) — see dossier §3.3.
The refusal, the murmuring, and the oath barring the generation; Caleb, Joshua and the little ones excepted (Num 14:30–31).
The presumptuous attack and the defeat by the Amalekites and Canaanites at Hormah.
Moses barred from the land: Deuteronomy attributes it to the people's sake; Numbers to Meribah. The tension is recorded, not resolved (dossier §3.3, clm-deu-01-028).
“Forty years didst thou sustain them in the wilderness, so that they lacked nothing” — the same forty years, the same provision.
Paul's summary: “about the time of forty years suffered he their manners in the wilderness.”
Moab and Ammon as the children of Lot — the kinship behind the sparing (repeated at Deut 2:19).
The Emim and Horim as ancient peoples: Gen 14:5 names the Rephaim, Zuzim, Emim and Horites in the days of Abraham.
The Caphtorim from Caphtor; Amos 9:7 recalls the Philistines brought from Caphtor — the same Caphtor tradition.
Sihon: the peace embassy, the refusal, the battle at Jahaz, the taking of his cities.
Jephthah's rehearsal of the Sihon embassy, agreeing with Deuteronomy's version.

“This day will I begin to put the dread of thee… upon the nations” — as the Song of the Sea anticipated (“the inhabitants of Palestina shall be afraid… all the inhabitants of Canaan shall melt away”).
The herem command (“thou shalt utterly destroy them”) behind the herem language of 2:34 (repeated at 3:6); Category 3.
Og: the battle at Edrei, the total defeat, the sixty cities (Num 21:35; Deut 3:3–4).
The summary of the two Amorite kings, Sihon and Og, and the land from Arnon to Hermon.
The Transjordan allotment to Reuben, Gad and half-Manasseh, with the armed-vanguard condition (Num 32:20–22, 28–33).
Joshua restates the vanguard condition to the eastern tribes at the crossing.
“Charge Joshua, and encourage him, and strengthen him” — the commissioning of Joshua before Eleazar and the congregation.
“Get thee up into the top of Pisgah” — the command to ascend and view the land (Num 27:12, “Get thee up into this mount Abarim”).
The Pisgah/Nebo command repeated at the book's end (Category 9).
Moses' exclusion: “They angered him also at the waters of strife, so that it went ill with Moses for their sakes” (JFB cites Ps 106:32–33 on Deut 1:37).
“Who smote great nations, and slew mighty kings; Sihon king of the Amorites…” — the victory as praise.
“To him which smote great kings… Sihon king of the Amorites… Og the king of Bashan… and gave their land for an heritage” — the victory as praise.

“Moreover thou gavest them kingdoms and nations… so they possessed the land of Sihon, and the land of the king of Heshbon, and the land of Og king of Bashan” — the confession's summary of Deut 2:24–3:10.
“They could not enter in because of unbelief” — the wilderness generation's unbelief as the reason for exclusion (JFB cites Heb 3:19 on Deut 1:28).
“Ye shall not respect persons in judgment… for the judgment is God's” — echoed in Jehoshaphat's charge: “ye judge not for man, but for the LORD.”
Horeb, “the mountain of God,” where Moses saw the burning bush — the mountain the journey starts from.
The Anakim the spies feared are cut off by Joshua “from the mountains” — the later fulfilment of what the spies dreaded.
Kadesh: Miriam died and was buried there, and Moses brought water from the rock at Meribah — the halt's other events (cf. BAR on Kadesh-barnea).
